repairs.q: Nominal GDP rises while quantities are unchanged. Does that prove production increased?
options: No; higher current prices can raise nominal GDP
Yes; nominal GDP measures only changes in physical quantities
Yes; every nominal increase establishes the same real growth
No; nominal GDP deliberately excludes every change in prices
repairs.feedback: Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production.

repairs.q: Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?
options: Yes; subtract the inflation percentage directly from the nominal dollar level
Yes; but only when the measured inflation rate remains positive
No; value current quantities at current prices in both measures
No; value current quantities at consistent base-year prices
repairs.feedback: Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods.

repairs.q: If beef gets expensive and consumers buy more chicken, the CPI may:
options: Overstate the rise in cost of living
Perfectly capture the change
Measure unemployment instead
Ignore all food
repairs.feedback: The fixed CPI basket may miss substitution toward cheaper chicken.

repairs.q: Substitution bias happens because consumers:
options: Switch toward relatively cheaper goods
Never respond to prices
Only buy imports
Stop buying all goods
repairs.feedback: Consumers substitute toward goods that become relatively cheaper.

repairs.q: A demand increase raises inflation and lowers unemployment while expectations are unchanged. Is this a movement or a shift?
options: A movement along the current SRPC
An upward shift of the entire SRPC
A leftward shift of the LRPC
A downward shift of the entire SRPC
repairs.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

repairs.q: Expected inflation rises while unemployment is held fixed. What happens to the SRPC?
options: The economy moves up the same SRPC
It shifts downward
The LRPC becomes horizontal
It shifts upward
repairs.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

repairs.q: On a Phillips graph, moving upward and left along one SRPC means what?
options: Inflation falls while unemployment rises
Inflation and unemployment both fall
Inflation rises while unemployment falls
Inflation and unemployment both rise
repairs.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

repairs.q: Can a downward-sloping SRPC guarantee permanently lower unemployment from higher inflation?
options: No, because demand never affects unemployment
No, because expected inflation adjusts
Yes, because the same SRPC is permanent
Yes, because natural unemployment becomes zero
repairs.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

repairs.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation and unemployment together. What curve change is indicated?
options: An upward shift of the SRPC
Movement up-left along the same SRPC
A downward shift of the SRPC
A vertical movement along the LRPC
repairs.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

repairs.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
options: $30 billion.
$40 billion.
$10 billion.
$53.3 billion.
repairs.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.

repairs.q: Deposits are $1,000 and the reserve requirement is 10 percent. Required reserves are:
repairs.feedback: Required reserves equal deposits times the reserve requirement: $1,000 x 0.10 = $100.

repairs.q: Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
options: No; it rose more slowly
Yes; any inflation decline lowers prices
Yes; disinflation and deflation are identical
No; the price level stayed exactly fixed
repairs.feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

repairs.q: Contractionary disinflation raises unemployment in the short run. Is that necessarily permanent?
options: Yes; every contraction shifts LRPC right
Yes; the SRPC never shifts after policy
No; unemployment must fall below natural immediately
No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
repairs.feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

repairs.q: Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
options: Expected inflation adjusts and unemployment returns toward natural
Aggregate demand has no short-run effect
The natural rate always falls with inflation
Nominal wages never respond to prices
repairs.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

repairs.q: Structural unemployment falls because matching improves. Is that movement along or a shift of LRPC?
options: Movement upward along the LRPC
Movement left along a fixed LRPC
An upward shift of SRPC only
A leftward shift of the LRPC
repairs.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

repairs.q: Unions and efficiency wages can both create unemployment when they:
options: Keep wages above equilibrium
Lower wages below equilibrium
Eliminate labor supply
Make CPI rise
repairs.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor.

repairs.q: A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account. In a separate transaction, the Federal Reserve credits a bank’s reserve account during an asset purchase. Which distinction is correct?
options: The commercial bank creates a deposit liability; the Fed creates central-bank reserves
The Fed creates the borrower’s commercial-bank deposit, while the bank creates central-bank reserves
Both transactions create only physical currency held by the public
Neither transaction changes any bank liability or reserve balance
repairs.feedback: Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

repairs.q: A central-bank asset purchase sharply increases reserve balances, yet commercial-bank lending changes little. Which statement best separates the institutions’ roles?
options: The central bank failed to create any reserve balances because commercial banks did not expand loans after the asset purchase
Commercial banks create central-bank reserves whenever they choose not to lend
Reserve balances are identical to bank capital, so unchanged lending proves capital was unchanged
The central bank creates reserves; commercial-bank deposit creation still depends on lending and borrowing
repairs.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

repairs.q: If the reserve requirement is lowered, other things equal, what happens to the amount of deposits banks must hold as required reserves?
options: It falls, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending
It rises, leaving fewer reserves potentially available for lending
It is unchanged because reserve requirements affect only currency
It becomes equal to total bank capital
repairs.feedback: A lower reserve requirement reduces the amount of deposits that must be held as required reserves, leaving more reserves potentially available for lending.

repairs.feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right and can help close a recessionary gap.
